title: When short is enough: Comparing adaptive and fixed-item numerosity tests in early childhood
abstract: Understanding children's numerosity perception is essential for identifying the cognitive foundations of early mathematical learning, yet traditional assessment methods remain lengthy and inefficient. Adaptive testing has emerged as a promising alternative, offering precise ability estimates while reducing task length and participant burden. In adaptive tests, item difficulty is dynamically adjusted to match each participant's estimated ability, so items are neither too difficult nor too easy. Despite these advantages, few studies have applied adaptive testing to numerosity perception so far, and none have considered the multidimensional nature of the task, involving both numerical acuity and inhibitory control. This study compares an adaptive version of a numerosity comparison task with a long (128 items) and a short (48 items) fixed-item version in a sample of 146 children aged four to eight years ( M = 6.45). Task performance in the three versions was compared across several dimensions. Results showed that accuracy was correlated across the three versions, and all of them showed the expected congruency and ratio effects. Number was the strongest predictor compared to the non-numerical cues, and it affected performance similarly in all three versions. All versions also revealed three different cognitive profiles that classified children with high consistency. Finally, the measurement precision was comparable across versions. Importantly, the adaptive and the short versions also elicited lower state math anxiety, particularly among participants with higher math anxiety. These findings suggest that an adaptive numerosity comparison task could offer the same type of information while reducing test length and improving participant experience.
